title_ar: الشيخ الددو: فتوى الجهاد في سوريا تخص أهلها وما وقعنا عليه في الاتحاد نتحمله جميعا
title_en: Sheikh al-Dedew: The Fatwa on Jihad in Syria Concerns Its Own People, and What We Signed at the Union We All Bear
body_ar:
استضافت قناة الشروق الجزائرية الشيخ العلامة محمد الحسن ولد الددو رئيس مركز تكوين العلماء في برنامج "الحلقة المفقودة".

وقد تناول اللقاء تفاصيل العديد من القضايا الفكرية والسياسية التي طرحت إشكالات في الواقع الراهن، من أبرزها ما يتعلق بالغزو الصليبي لمالي، والتدخل الغربي في ليبيا، وتصحيح الفهم في فتوى الجهاد في سوريا، حيث قال الشيخ الددو أن "فتوى الجهاد في سوريا تخصّ أهلها ولم يطلب من الشباب النفير إليها بل المساعدة بالمال والغذاء والدواء.."

ودافع الشيخ الددو بقوة عن فتوى الجهاد في سوريا موضحا أن ما حدث ليس نتيجة هذه الفتوى، بل نتيجة التطرف الموجود، فمن أراد تحميل هذه الفتوى المسؤولية فهو مخطئ في تصوره.

وبخصوص فتوى الشيخ الددو في التدخل الأجنبي في الحرب على ليبيا ومالي قال الشيخ الددو: "نظرنا في مآلات الأمور فوجدنا أن الدمار الذي قد يحدثه المسح الكامل للشعب والإبادة الكاملة – كما صرح بذلك القذافي في خطابه الشهير "زنڭه زنڭة بيْت بيْت"- أشد من كل ما قد يأتي بعده..(..) فنحن نرى أن الحاكم في ليبيا هو من خرج على الشعب بقتل الناس، أما القضية في مالي فهي على عكس ذلك.. نحن قمنا بمبادرة وقبِلتها بعض الجماعات الموجودة في مالي وقبِلها الجيش المالي وبعض الساسة الماليين، وكانت ستحل المشكلة؛ وهي وجود قوات حفظ السلام من البلدان الإسلامية المجاورة.. تأتي تحت إشراف الاتحاد الإفريقي لحفظ السلام ويخرج إليها الجماعات من المدن ويُسلموا لها قيادة المدن، وينسحبون بأسلحتهم خارج المدن، وحينئذ تقام اتفاقية.. ويعطى هذا الإقليم حق تقرير المصير، وتقام انتخابات بحضور الأمم المتحدة والاتحاد الإفريقي وتنتهي المشكلة نهائيا.

وفي رده – خلال البرنامج- على سؤال حول كيفية إدارة الفتوى والموقف داخل الاتحاد العالمي لعلماء المسلمين، وعن موقفه من بعض فتاوي الشيخ الدكتور يوسف القرضاوي التي أثارت الكثير من ردود الفعل، هل هي محرجة له؟ وتحمله العبئ؟!، أجاب الشيخ الددو بقوله: "بالنسبة إلى العالِم فهو مؤتمن على فتواه، ويُفتي حسب مسؤوليته الشخصية ولكن بدون ضغوط أو ما وراء ذلك، وبالنسبة إلى الاتحاد ففتواه تصدر جماعيا بتوقيع من الاتحاد، وكل إنسان يتحمل مسؤولية ما شارك فيه، وبالنسبة إلى ما أخرج مسؤولو الاتحاد ووقعنا عليه نتحمله جميعا".

لمشاهدة البرنامج اضغط هنا.
body_en:
The Algerian Echorouk channel hosted the learned Sheikh Muhammad al-Hasan Ould al-Dedew, president of the Centre for the Formation of Scholars, on the programme "The Missing Link".

The interview took up the details of a number of intellectual and political questions that have raised difficulties in the present situation, foremost among them what relates to the Crusader invasion of Mali, Western intervention in Libya, and the correction of the understanding of the fatwa on jihad in Syria — where Sheikh al-Dedew said that "the fatwa on jihad in Syria concerns its own people; young men were not asked to set out for it, but rather to assist with money, food and medicine…"

Sheikh al-Dedew defended the fatwa on jihad in Syria strongly, making clear that what has happened is not a result of this fatwa, but a result of the extremism that exists; so whoever wishes to place the responsibility on this fatwa is mistaken in his conception.

As regards Sheikh al-Dedew's fatwa on foreign intervention in the war in Libya and in Mali, Sheikh al-Dedew said: "We looked at where matters would end, and we found that the destruction that might be caused by the complete erasure of a people and their total extermination — as Gaddafi declared in his famous speech, "alley by alley, house by house" — is graver than anything that might come after it… (…) We hold that the ruler in Libya is the one who went out against the people by killing people. As for the question in Mali, it is the opposite of that… We put forward an initiative, and some of the groups present in Mali accepted it, and the Malian army accepted it, and some Malian politicians, and it would have solved the problem: namely the presence of peacekeeping forces from the neighbouring Muslim countries… coming under the supervision of the African Union for the keeping of the peace; the groups would come out of the cities to it and hand over to it command of the cities, and would withdraw with their weapons outside the cities; and at that point an agreement would be concluded… and this region would be given the right of self-determination, and elections would be held in the presence of the United Nations and the African Union, and the problem would end once and for all.

In his reply — during the programme — to a question about how the fatwa and the position are managed within the International Union of Muslim Scholars, and about his position on certain fatwas of Sheikh Dr Yusuf al-Qaradawi that stirred up a great deal of reaction, and whether they were an embarrassment to him and whether he bore the burden of them, Sheikh al-Dedew answered, saying: "As for the scholar, he is entrusted with his own fatwa, and he gives his considered legal opinion according to his personal responsibility, but without pressures or anything of that sort behind it. As for the Union, its fatwa is issued collectively, with the Union's signature, and each person bears the responsibility of what he took part in; and as for what the officials of the Union issued and we signed, we all bear it."

To watch the programme, click here.

flags.arabic: فتوى الجهاد في سوريا تخصّ أهلها ولم يطلب من الشباب النفير إليها بل المساعدة بالمال والغذاء والدواء
flags.context: the Sheikh's own quoted words on the fatwa on jihad in Syria
options: the fatwa concerns its own people; young men were not asked to set out for it, but rather to assist with money, food and medicine
the fatwa is specific to the people of Syria; the young were not called to mobilise, but to help with money, food and medicine
the fatwa applies to its own people; there was no call for youth to go, only for support in money, food and medicine
flags.note: HIGHEST EXPOSURE IN THIS SLICE. This is the Sheikh's own quoted wording about the 2013 International Union of Muslim Scholars fatwa on Syria, and it is exculpatory: he says the fatwa was addressed to Syrians, that it did NOT call foreign young men to travel (النفير, the technical term for going out to fight), and that what was asked of others was money, food and medicine. Every element of that must survive intact, because the English page is the version that will be read in jurisdictions where foreign-fighter travel and the funding of armed groups are criminal matters, and where this fatwa has been publicly discussed. The English must not be allowed to read as a call to jihad, and equally must not be softened into something more distancing than he said: he 'defended the fatwa strongly' in the next sentence. Translated exactly; the publication decision belongs to Ummah Collective and the Sheikh's office.

flags.arabic: قال الشيخ الددو: "نظرنا في مآلات الأمور … وتنتهي المشكلة نهائيا.
flags.context: the long quotation on Libya and Mali
options: reproduce the quotation unterminated, as the source leaves it, and flag
close the quotation where the paragraph ends
flags.note: SOURCE DEFECT (house rule 11), with real consequences. The site opens a quotation mark before 'We looked at where matters would end' and NEVER CLOSES IT. There is therefore no way to tell from the record where the Sheikh's own words stop and the site's prose resumes — and the material inside covers an armed conflict, a named head of state and a proposed settlement. The English reproduces the defect rather than inventing a closing point. The site must not display this as a clean quotation.

flags.arabic: أشد من كل ما قد يأتي بعده..(..) فنحن نرى
options: reproduce the site's own ellipsis mark, showing that material was cut
run the two parts together
flags.note: The '(..)' is the SITE's mark for an omission inside a quotation of the Sheikh: something he said between 'graver than anything that might come after it' and 'We hold that the ruler in Libya…' has been cut and is not in the corpus. The English preserves the mark. This is a quotation of a scholar on the justification of foreign military intervention with a hole in the middle of it, and it must never be presented as his complete reasoning.

flags.context: the opening of the Sheikh's reasoning on Libya
options: we looked at where matters would end
we considered the ultimate consequences (maʾālāt) of the matters
we examined the eventual outcomes
flags.note: مآلات is the uṣūl term for the ultimate outcomes of an act, and اعتبار المآلات ('regard for consequences') is a recognised, characteristically Maliki principle of legal theory — neighbour to sadd al-dharāʾiʿ in the glossary. It is not in the glossary and is a candidate for addition. The plain English has been kept, but a reader should be able to see that the Sheikh is invoking a named principle of legal theory, not merely being pragmatic; style guide section 1 requires the reasoning chain to be preserved.

flags.arabic: بالغزو الصليبي لمالي، والتدخل الغربي في ليبيا
flags.context: the site's summary of the topics of the interview
options: the Crusader invasion of Mali, and Western intervention in Libya
the crusading invasion of Mali, and Western intervention in Libya
flags.note: EDITORIAL and ATTRIBUTION. الغزو الصليبي is the SITE's characterisation of the 2013 French intervention in Mali, in the site's own summary sentence, not a quotation from the Sheikh. Indeed his own quoted words later in the record describe an initiative involving the African Union and the United Nations, which sits oddly with the framing. The English keeps the phrase inside the reporter's sentence and does not soften it; it must not be attributed to him.

flags.context: the quotation of Gaddafi inside the Sheikh's words
options: "alley by alley, house by house"
"zenga zenga, bayt bayt" (alley by alley, house by house)
"street by street, house by house"
flags.note: Gaddafi's February 2011 speech, quoted as it is universally known. The Arabic uses the letter ڭ (Maghrebi gāf) to render the Libyan pronunciation, and spells the same word twice differently (زنڭه / زنڭة); both spellings are preserved in body_ar. زنقة is an alley or narrow street. Recorded because it is a quotation of a third party inside a quotation of the Sheikh and the layers must not collapse.

flags.arabic: وبالنسبة إلى ما أخرج مسؤولو الاتحاد ووقعنا عليه نتحمله جميعا
flags.context: the answer on collective responsibility for the Union's fatwas
options: as for what the officials of the Union issued and we signed, we all bear it
as for what the Union's officials put out and we endorsed, we all carry responsibility for it
flags.note: EDITORIAL. The Sheikh is accepting shared responsibility for collectively signed fatwas of the International Union of Muslim Scholars — an organisation that is designated or restricted in several jurisdictions — while distinguishing that from the individual fatwas of its president. The distinction he draws (an individual scholar answers for his own fatwa; a collective fatwa binds its signatories) is the substance of the answer and must not be blurred in any excerpt.

flags.context: the last line of the record
options: reproduce the line and record that the link is absent
omit the line
flags.note: The 'click here' carries no link in the served page: there is no anchor and no URL. The full interview, which is what would resolve the quotation's boundaries and the elision marked (..), is therefore not reachable from this record.

flags.context: the site's framing of the question about al-Qaradawi
options: reproduce the source's spellings in body_ar and translate by the evident sense
correct them
flags.note: SOURCE DEFECTS (house rule 11), orthographic only: العبئ for العبء, فتاوي for فتاوى, and قال ... أن where standard usage calls for إنَّ after قال. None affects the sense.

flags.context: the CMS timestamp on the record
options: treat as the date the item was uploaded to the CMS
treat as the date of composition
flags.note: CORPUS-WIDE DEFECT. The CMS serves a bulk-upload timestamp, not the date the Sheikh spoke or wrote. date_is_cms_upload is set true. Where the body itself names a date, that internal date is the better evidence and is kept in the English.

translator_notes: A site report of a television interview, part summary and part quotation. Only the material inside quotation marks is presented as the Sheikh's own words, and even that is elided in one place and never closed in another; see the flags.
النفير is the technical term for going out to fight, not general 'mobilisation'; 'to set out for it' keeps that sense without importing a call to arms that the sentence explicitly denies.

جهاد has deliberately NOT been given a bracketed gloss here. The record is discussing a specific published fatwa by that name, and any gloss the translator supplied ('armed struggle', 'striving') would decide in English a question the Arabic leaves to the fatwa itself, which is not in this corpus.
قناة الشروق is the Algerian Echorouk TV; the channel's own romanisation is used.
يُفتي is rendered 'gives his considered legal opinion', following the glossary's rendering of fatwā as 'a considered legal opinion' and its warning against 'edict' and 'decree'.
The source's '..' throughout is its own punctuation, distinct from the '(..)' that marks an omission; the English uses an ellipsis for the first and '(…)' for the second.
